description: Extensive question bank derived from 'Environmental Geography and Ecology' study material. Verify and expand questions before formal examination use.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: According to the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, environment is defined as the inter-relationship among which components?

options.A: Water, air, land, human beings, other living creatures, plants, micro-organisms and property
options.D: Only living organisms and their habitats

questions.explanation: The Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 defines environment broadly through the inter-relationship among water, air, land, human beings, other living creatures, plants, micro-organisms and property.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following is the correct definition of environment?

options.A: Only the natural surroundings of an organism
options.B: The sum of external physical, chemical, biological and human-made conditions that surround organisms and influence their life, development and activities
options.C: Only the biotic components of an ecosystem
options.D: The built environment created by humans

questions.explanation: Environment is the sum of external physical, chemical, biological and human-made conditions that surround organisms and influence their life, development and activities.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which sphere of the Earth environment includes the solid outer Earth, crust and uppermost mantle?
questions.explanation: The lithosphere is the solid outer Earth, including the crust and uppermost mantle. It provides the physical base for terrestrial life.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which sphere includes all water in liquid, solid and vapour forms?
questions.explanation: The hydrosphere includes all water in liquid, solid and vapour forms—oceans, rivers, lakes, groundwater, glaciers and atmospheric water.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which sphere is the envelope of gases around the Earth?
questions.explanation: The atmosphere is the envelope of gases around the Earth. It provides weather, climate, oxygen, carbon dioxide and protection from harmful radiation.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which sphere is the global zone of life and its interactions?
questions.explanation: The biosphere is the global zone of life and its interactions, including organisms and ecosystems across land, water and lower atmosphere.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following is an example of a human-made environment?
questions.explanation: Dams, industries, settlements, roads, farms and ports are human-made or built environment features created or substantially modified by people.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following is an example of a natural environment feature?
questions.explanation: The natural environment consists of features and processes formed mainly by nature, such as mountains, rivers, climate, soils, forests and wildlife.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What are biotic components?

options.B: Living organisms—plants, animals, fungi and micro-organisms

questions.explanation: Biotic components are living organisms—plants, animals, fungi and micro-organisms.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following is an abiotic component?
questions.explanation: Abiotic components are non-living physical and chemical factors such as sunlight, temperature, water, air, soil, minerals, salinity and pH.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which biotic group manufactures organic matter, usually by photosynthesis?
questions.explanation: Producers (autotrophs) manufacture organic matter, usually by photosynthesis.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which biotic group obtains energy by eating organisms or organic matter?
questions.explanation: Consumers obtain energy by eating organisms or organic matter.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which biotic group breaks down dead material and wastes, returning nutrients to the environment?
questions.explanation: Decomposers and detritivores break down dead material and wastes, returning nutrients to the environment.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following is an example of environmental interaction?
questions.explanation: Environmental interaction includes plant uptake of soil nutrients, transpiration affecting atmospheric moisture, rivers transporting sediments and human land-use change altering habitats.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: How do the four Earth spheres interact?

options.A: They are isolated and do not interact
options.B: Matter and energy move continuously among them through processes like the water cycle and volcanic eruptions
options.C: Only the atmosphere and hydrosphere interact
options.D: Only the biosphere interacts with other spheres

questions.explanation: The four spheres are not isolated; matter and energy move continuously among them. Examples include the water cycle linking all spheres and volcanic eruptions transferring material from the lithosphere to the atmosphere.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Why is the environment considered a dynamic system?

options.B: Because it changes only through human actions
options.C: Because it changes through natural processes and human actions such as urbanisation, extraction, pollution, deforestation and conservation
options.D: Because it is static and unchanging

questions.explanation: The environment changes through natural processes—weather, erosion, succession, volcanic activity and climate variability—and through human actions such as urbanisation, extraction, pollution, deforestation and conservation.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What is an ecosystem?

options.A: A group of organisms of the same species
options.B: A functional unit of nature in which a community of organisms interacts with one another and with the non-living environment through energy flow and nutrient cycling
options.C: Only the physical environment of an area

questions.explanation: An ecosystem is a functional unit of nature in which a community of organisms interacts with one another and with the non-living environment through energy flow and nutrient cycling.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following is an example of an ecosystem?
questions.explanation: An ecosystem may be small, such as a pond, or extensive, such as a forest or ocean.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What does the structure of an ecosystem include?

options.B: Abiotic components, biotic components, trophic levels, food chains and food webs, and spatial features

questions.explanation: Ecosystem structure includes abiotic components; biotic components (producers, consumers and decomposers); trophic levels; food chains and food webs; and spatial features such as vegetation layers or aquatic zones.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What are the major functions of an ecosystem?

options.B: Productivity, energy transfer, decomposition and nutrient cycling

questions.explanation: Major functions include productivity (formation of biomass), energy transfer through trophic levels, decomposition of organic matter, and cycling of nutrients such as carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus and water. Ecosystems also provide habitat and regulate environmental processes.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Differentiate primary productivity and secondary productivity.

options.A: Primary productivity is biomass production by consumers; secondary productivity is by producers
options.B: Primary productivity is the rate at which producers create organic matter; secondary productivity is biomass production by consumers
options.D: Primary productivity is energy transfer; secondary productivity is nutrient cycling

questions.explanation: Primary productivity is the rate at which producers create organic matter. Secondary productivity is biomass production by consumers.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What is Gross Primary Productivity (GPP)?
questions.explanation: Gross primary productivity (GPP) is total photosynthetic production.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What is Net Primary Productivity (NPP)?
questions.explanation: Net primary productivity (NPP) is GPP minus plant respiration.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following are producers?

options.A: Green plants, algae and photosynthetic bacteria
options.C: Bacteria and fungi that break down dead matter

questions.explanation: Producers include green plants, algae and photosynthetic bacteria.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following are decomposers?

options.C: Bacteria and fungi that chemically break down dead organic matter

questions.explanation: Decomposers—especially bacteria and fungi—chemically break down dead organic matter; detritivores such as earthworms fragment it.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following is an example of a food chain?
questions.explanation: A food chain is a linear pathway of energy transfer through feeding relationships. Example: grass → grasshopper → frog → snake → eagle.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What is a food web?

options.A: A single linear pathway of energy transfer
options.B: A network of interconnected food chains
options.C: A diagram showing trophic levels by biomass

questions.explanation: A food web is a network of interconnected food chains. It is generally more realistic than a single chain because most organisms use more than one food source and may be eaten by several predators.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What are trophic levels?

options.A: Feeding positions in a food chain

questions.explanation: Trophic levels are feeding positions in a food chain: first level—producers; second—primary consumers; third—secondary consumers; fourth—tertiary consumers. Omnivores may occupy more than one level.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which trophic level is occupied by green plants?
questions.explanation: Producers occupy the first trophic level.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which ecological pyramid is always upright?
questions.explanation: Pyramids of energy are always upright because usable energy decreases at each transfer. Pyramids of number or biomass may be upright or inverted depending on the ecosystem.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which pyramid can be inverted, for example, when one tree supports many insects?
questions.explanation: Pyramids of number may be inverted, e.g. one tree supporting many insects.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: In which ecosystem can the pyramid of biomass be inverted because phytoplankton have low standing biomass but rapid turnover?
questions.explanation: Biomass pyramids can be inverted in some aquatic systems because phytoplankton have low standing biomass but rapid turnover.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: The 10 per cent law of energy transfer is associated with:
questions.explanation: Raymond Lindeman's ecological rule of thumb states that, on average, only about 10% of energy at one trophic level is transferred to the next.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following statements about the 10 per cent law is correct?

options.A: It is an exact law applicable to every food chain
options.B: It is an approximation, not a fixed universal percentage
options.C: It states that 90% of energy is transferred to the next trophic level
options.D: It applies only to aquatic ecosystems

questions.explanation: The 10 per cent law is an approximation, not a fixed universal percentage. Much energy is used in respiration, movement and maintenance or remains uneaten.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: How does energy flow through an ecosystem?

options.B: Energy flows one way and is ultimately dissipated as heat; it is not recycled
options.C: Energy flows in both directions between trophic levels
options.D: Energy is stored permanently in biomass

questions.explanation: Energy enters mainly as sunlight, is captured by producers, passes to consumers and decomposers, and is ultimately dissipated as heat. Energy flow is one-way and requires continual input; unlike nutrients, energy is not recycled.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What is ecological succession?

options.A: The gradual change in species composition and community structure over time
options.B: The movement of energy through trophic levels
options.C: The cycling of nutrients in an ecosystem

questions.explanation: Ecological succession is the gradual change in species composition and community structure over time.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Primary succession begins on:
questions.explanation: Primary succession begins on a surface lacking developed soil, such as new lava or bare rock.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Secondary succession occurs where:

options.B: A community was disturbed but soil or biological legacies remain

questions.explanation: Secondary succession occurs where a community was disturbed but soil or biological legacies remain. It often follows disturbance such as fire, cultivation or storm.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which succession type is usually slower?
questions.explanation: Primary succession starts without pre-existing soil and is usually slower. Secondary succession recovery is often faster because soil, seeds or roots may remain.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What are pioneer species?

options.B: Early colonisers of a newly available or disturbed habitat

questions.explanation: Pioneer species are early colonisers of a newly available or disturbed habitat.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What is a climax community?

options.A: The first species to colonise an area
options.B: The relatively persistent late-successional community under prevailing conditions
options.C: A community that has been destroyed by fire
options.D: A community of only pioneer species

questions.explanation: A climax community is the relatively persistent late-successional community under prevailing conditions. Modern ecology recognises that disturbances and environmental change can prevent a single permanent climax.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What is nutrient cycling?

options.A: The one-way flow of energy through trophic levels
options.B: The movement and reuse of chemical elements between organisms and abiotic reservoirs

questions.explanation: Nutrient cycling is the movement and reuse of chemical elements between organisms and abiotic reservoirs through processes such as uptake, feeding, excretion, decomposition, weathering and atmospheric exchange.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: In the carbon cycle, which process returns carbon to the atmosphere from organisms?
questions.explanation: In the carbon cycle, respiration and decomposition return carbon to air or water. Photosynthesis absorbs carbon dioxide.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following adds substantial CO2 to the atmosphere in the carbon cycle?

options.B: Combustion of fossil fuels, cement production and land-use change

questions.explanation: Combustion of fossil fuels, cement production and land-use change add substantial CO2 to the atmosphere.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which process converts atmospheric nitrogen into biologically usable forms?
questions.explanation: Nitrogen fixation converts atmospheric N2 into biologically usable forms (by microbes, lightning or industry).

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which process converts ammonium to nitrite and nitrate in the nitrogen cycle?
questions.explanation: Nitrification converts ammonium to nitrite and nitrate.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which process returns organic nitrogen to ammonium in the nitrogen cycle?
questions.explanation: Ammonification returns organic nitrogen to ammonium.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which process returns nitrate-derived nitrogen to N2 or other gases?
questions.explanation: Denitrification returns nitrate-derived nitrogen to N2 or other gases.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: In the oxygen cycle, which process releases oxygen?
questions.explanation: Photosynthesis releases oxygen; respiration, decomposition and combustion consume it.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which processes consume oxygen in the oxygen cycle?
questions.explanation: Respiration, decomposition and combustion consume oxygen. Oxygen also participates in oxidation and chemical reactions in air, water and rocks.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What drives evaporation and transpiration in the water cycle?
questions.explanation: Solar energy drives evaporation and transpiration; water vapour condenses into clouds and returns as precipitation.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following is a process in the water cycle?
questions.explanation: The water cycle includes evaporation, transpiration, condensation, precipitation, infiltration, runoff, sublimation and groundwater discharge.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What are terrestrial ecosystems?

options.B: Ecosystems that occur on land and are strongly influenced by climate and soil

questions.explanation: Terrestrial ecosystems occur on land and are strongly influenced by climate and soil.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What are aquatic ecosystems influenced by?

options.B: Salinity, depth, light, temperature, dissolved oxygen and water movement

questions.explanation: Aquatic ecosystems occur in water and are influenced by salinity, depth, light, temperature, dissolved oxygen and water movement.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which ecosystem is dominated by trees and layered vegetation with high habitat complexity?
questions.explanation: Forest ecosystems are dominated by trees and layered vegetation, with high habitat complexity.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which ecosystem is dominated by grasses and herbs, often maintained by rainfall patterns, grazing and fire?
questions.explanation: Grasslands are dominated by grasses and herbs, often maintained by rainfall patterns, grazing and fire.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which ecosystem has low and irregular precipitation, with organisms showing water-conservation and heat-avoidance adaptations?
questions.explanation: Deserts have low and irregular precipitation; organisms show water-conservation and heat-avoidance adaptations.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following is a marine ecosystem?
questions.explanation: Marine ecosystems have saline water and include oceans, coral reefs, estuaries and coastal habitats.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following is a freshwater ecosystem?
questions.explanation: Freshwater ecosystems have low dissolved salts and include rivers, streams, lakes, ponds and wetlands.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What are lentic ecosystems?

options.A: Flowing waters such as rivers and streams
options.B: Standing waters such as lakes and ponds
options.C: Coastal zones where freshwater mixes with seawater
options.D: Areas where water saturates the soil

questions.explanation: Lentic systems are standing waters such as lakes and ponds.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What are lotic ecosystems?

options.A: Standing waters such as lakes and ponds
options.B: Flowing waters such as rivers and streams

questions.explanation: Lotic systems are flowing waters such as rivers and streams.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What are wetlands?

options.A: Areas where water saturates or covers the soil permanently or seasonally, supporting hydric soils and water-adapted vegetation

questions.explanation: Wetlands are areas where water saturates or covers the soil permanently or seasonally, supporting hydric soils and water-adapted vegetation.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What is an estuary?

options.B: A coastal zone where river freshwater mixes with seawater

questions.explanation: An estuary is a coastal zone where river freshwater mixes with seawater.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Why are estuaries highly productive?

options.A: Because of nutrient inputs, shallow waters and sheltered habitats
options.C: Because they are deep and dark
options.D: Because they have high salinity only

questions.explanation: Nutrient inputs, shallow waters and sheltered habitats often support high productivity, nursery grounds for fish and important bird habitats in estuaries.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What are ecosystem services?

options.C: Only the economic value of forests

questions.explanation: Ecosystem services are benefits people obtain from ecosystems: provisioning, regulating, cultural and supporting services.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which category of ecosystem services includes food, freshwater and timber?
questions.explanation: Provisioning services include food, freshwater and timber.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which category of ecosystem services includes climate, flood and disease regulation?
questions.explanation: Regulating services include climate, flood and disease regulation.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which category of ecosystem services includes recreation, spiritual and educational value?
questions.explanation: Cultural services include recreation, spiritual and educational value.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which category of ecosystem services includes soil formation, nutrient cycling and primary production?
questions.explanation: Supporting or underlying processes include soil formation, nutrient cycling and primary production.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What is biodiversity?

options.A: Only the number of species in an area
options.B: The variability among living organisms from all sources and the ecological complexes of which they are part
options.C: Only genetic variation within a species

questions.explanation: Biodiversity is the variability among living organisms from all sources and the ecological complexes of which they are part. It includes diversity within species, between species and of ecosystems.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Differentiate genetic, species and ecosystem diversity.

options.A: Genetic diversity is variation in genes within a species; species diversity is the variety and relative abundance of species; ecosystem diversity is the variety of habitats, communities and ecological processes
options.B: Genetic diversity is the variety of species; species diversity is variation in genes; ecosystem diversity is the variety of habitats
options.C: All three refer to the same thing
options.D: Genetic diversity refers to ecosystems; species diversity refers to genes

questions.explanation: Genetic diversity is variation in genes within a species or population; species diversity concerns the variety and relative abundance of species; ecosystem diversity is the variety of habitats, communities and ecological processes in a region.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What is a biodiversity hotspot?

options.A: A protected area with high biodiversity
options.B: A biogeographic region with exceptional plant endemism and severe habitat loss

questions.explanation: A globally recognised hotspot is a biogeographic region with exceptional plant endemism and severe habitat loss.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: According to Conservation International criteria, a biodiversity hotspot must have at least how many endemic vascular plant species?
questions.explanation: The widely used Conservation International criteria require at least 1,500 endemic vascular plant species and loss of at least 70% of original natural vegetation.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: According to Conservation International criteria, a biodiversity hotspot must have lost at least what percentage of its original natural vegetation?
questions.explanation: The criteria require loss of at least 70% of original natural vegetation.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which biodiversity hotspot includes the Nicobar Islands as the Indian part?
questions.explanation: The Nicobar Islands form the Indian part of the Sundaland hotspot.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the four global biodiversity hotspots that include parts of India?
questions.explanation: Four global hotspots include parts of India: Himalaya, Indo-Burma, Western Ghats-Sri Lanka, and Sundaland. The Atlantic Forest is in South America.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What is an endemic species?

options.A: A species found all over the world
options.B: A species native to and restricted to a particular geographic area

questions.explanation: An endemic species is native to and restricted to a particular geographic area.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following is an example of an endemic species associated with the Western Ghats?
questions.explanation: Examples associated with the Western Ghats include the lion-tailed macaque and Nilgiri tahr.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What does 'extinct' mean in the IUCN Red List context?

options.A: A species at high risk of extinction
options.B: No reasonable doubt that the last individual has died

questions.explanation: Extinct means no reasonable doubt that the last individual has died.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which IUCN categories are collectively termed 'threatened'?
questions.explanation: Critically Endangered (CR), Endangered (EN) and Vulnerable (VU) are collectively termed threatened.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following is the correct order of IUCN Red List categories from highest to lowest extinction risk?
questions.explanation: The IUCN Red List categories in order of increasing extinction risk include Least Concern (LC), Near Threatened (NT), Vulnerable (VU), Endangered (EN) and Critically Endangered (CR).

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What is an invasive alien species?

options.B: A non-native organism whose introduction or spread causes, or is likely to cause, environmental, economic or health harm
options.C: Any native species that is threatened
options.D: A species that is endemic to an area

questions.explanation: An invasive alien species is a non-native organism whose introduction or spread causes, or is likely to cause, environmental, economic or health harm. Not every alien species becomes invasive.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following is an example of an invasive alien species in India?
questions.explanation: Examples in India include water hyacinth, Lantana camara and Prosopis juliflora in affected landscapes.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following is a major threat to biodiversity?
questions.explanation: Major threats include habitat loss, degradation and fragmentation; overexploitation; invasive alien species; pollution; climate change; illegal wildlife trade; disease and unsustainable land- and water-use change.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What is in-situ conservation?

options.B: Conservation of species in their natural habitats

questions.explanation: In-situ conservation is conservation of species in their natural habitats, allowing ecological and evolutionary processes to continue.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following is an example of in-situ conservation?
questions.explanation: In-situ conservation examples include national parks, wildlife sanctuaries, conservation reserves, community reserves and biosphere reserves.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What is ex-situ conservation?
questions.explanation: Ex-situ conservation is conservation outside natural habitats, including botanical gardens, zoological parks, aquaria, seed banks, gene banks, field gene banks, tissue culture and captive-breeding programmes.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which is an example of ex-situ conservation?
questions.explanation: Seed banks conserve plant genetic material outside natural habitats.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which statement correctly differentiates a national park and a wildlife sanctuary in India?

options.A: Both are protected areas under the Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972, but national parks generally have stricter protection and rights are settled before final notification
options.B: National parks are not protected areas
options.C: Wildlife sanctuaries have no legal protection
options.D: National parks are only for plants

questions.explanation: Both are protected areas under the Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972. National parks generally have stricter protection and rights are settled before final notification; some regulated human activities may be permitted in sanctuaries subject to law and conditions.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What is a biosphere reserve?

options.A: A national park with strict protection
options.B: A large landscape or seascape recognised under UNESCO's Man and the Biosphere Programme to reconcile biodiversity conservation with sustainable use and research

questions.explanation: A biosphere reserve is a large landscape or seascape recognised under UNESCO's Man and the Biosphere Programme to reconcile biodiversity conservation with sustainable use and research.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What are the three zones commonly found in a biosphere reserve?
questions.explanation: A biosphere reserve commonly has core, buffer and transition zones. Designation as a biosphere reserve does not itself create a single uniform statutory protection category.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What is the difference between a biodiversity hotspot and a protected area?

options.A: A hotspot is a global priority region defined by endemism and habitat loss; a protected area is a legally or administratively designated site with defined conservation objectives
options.B: A hotspot is a legally designated site; a protected area is a global priority region
options.D: A hotspot is only in India; a protected area is global

questions.explanation: A hotspot is a global priority region defined by endemism and habitat loss; it may span several countries and contain both protected and unprotected land. A protected area is a legally or administratively designated site with defined conservation objectives.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which convention is primarily concerned with wetlands conservation and wise use?
questions.explanation: The Ramsar Convention (Convention on Wetlands) promotes conservation and wise use of wetlands.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What are the three objectives of the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD)?

options.A: Conservation of biological diversity; sustainable use of its components; fair and equitable sharing of benefits arising from genetic resources
options.B: Ozone protection, climate mitigation and desertification control
options.C: Trade regulation, pollution control and waste management
options.D: Wetland conservation, migratory species protection and heritage preservation

questions.explanation: The three objectives of the CBD are conservation of biological diversity; sustainable use of its components; and fair and equitable sharing of benefits arising from the utilisation of genetic resources.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What does CITES regulate?

options.B: International trade in listed species through appendices and permit systems

questions.explanation: CITES regulates international trade in listed species through appendices and permit systems. It does not simply ban all trade in all wildlife.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What is the difference between the IUCN and WWF?

options.A: IUCN is a membership union that produces scientific assessments including the Red List; WWF is an independent conservation organisation
options.B: IUCN is a UN treaty secretariat; WWF is a government agency
options.D: WWF produces the Red List; IUCN works on advocacy

questions.explanation: IUCN is a membership union of governments and civil-society organisations that produces scientific assessments, including the Red List. WWF is an independent conservation organisation. Neither is a UN treaty secretariat.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which protocol under the CBD concerns access and benefit-sharing?
questions.explanation: The Nagoya Protocol concerns access and benefit-sharing; the Cartagena Protocol concerns biosafety.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which protocol under the CBD concerns biosafety?
questions.explanation: The Cartagena Protocol concerns biosafety.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which convention concerns migratory species?
questions.explanation: The Convention on Migratory Species (CMS/Bonn Convention) is a major instrument with a distinct mandate concerning migratory species.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What is a natural resource?

options.B: A naturally occurring material, organism, energy flow or environmental condition that people value or use

questions.explanation: A natural resource is a naturally occurring material, organism, energy flow or environmental condition that people value or use, such as land, water, forests, minerals, sunlight and wind.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What are renewable resources?

options.A: Resources that form too slowly to be replenished within human timescales
options.B: Resources replenished naturally on human timescales if use remains within regeneration limits

questions.explanation: Renewable resources are replenished naturally on human timescales if use remains within regeneration limits, e.g. sunlight, wind and sustainably managed forests. Renewable does not mean inexhaustible.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What are non-renewable resources?

options.B: Resources that form too slowly to be replenished within human timescales

questions.explanation: Non-renewable resources form too slowly to be replenished within human timescales, e.g. coal, petroleum and many mineral deposits.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following is a renewable resource?
questions.explanation: Sunlight, wind and sustainably managed forests are renewable resources.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following is a non-renewable resource?
questions.explanation: Coal, petroleum and many mineral deposits are non-renewable resources.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What are the main pressures on land resources?

options.A: Soil erosion, salinisation, compaction, contamination, mining, urban sprawl, deforestation and desertification

questions.explanation: Pressures on land resources include soil erosion, salinisation, compaction, contamination, mining, urban sprawl, deforestation and desertification.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: How are water resources classified?

options.A: Surface water, groundwater, glaciers and rainwater

questions.explanation: Water resources include surface water (rivers, lakes, reservoirs and wetlands), groundwater, glaciers and rainwater.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following is a function of forest resources?

options.B: Carbon storage and soil and water regulation

questions.explanation: Forests provide timber, fuelwood, fodder, food, medicines, genetic resources, carbon storage, soil and water regulation, habitat and cultural values.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What are minerals?

options.B: Naturally occurring inorganic substances with characteristic chemical composition and structure

questions.explanation: Minerals are naturally occurring inorganic substances with characteristic chemical composition and structure.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following is a metallic mineral?
questions.explanation: Metallic minerals include iron ore, copper and bauxite. Limestone, mica and gypsum are non-metallic minerals.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following is a non-metallic mineral?
questions.explanation: Non-metallic minerals include limestone, mica and gypsum.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following is an energy mineral?
questions.explanation: Energy minerals include coal and uranium.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following is a renewable energy resource?
questions.explanation: Renewables include solar, wind, hydropower, biomass, geothermal and ocean energy.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following is a method of soil conservation?
questions.explanation: Soil conservation methods include contour ploughing, terracing, strip cropping, cover crops, crop rotation, mulching, shelter belts, afforestation, controlled grazing, gully plugging, check dams and conservation tillage.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following is a method of water conservation?
questions.explanation: Water conservation methods include rainwater harvesting, watershed development, recharge structures, protection of tanks and wetlands, drip and sprinkler irrigation, leakage reduction, wastewater treatment and reuse, crop planning and demand management.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What is sustainable development?

options.A: Development that meets present needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs
options.B: Development that exploits all resources now
options.C: Development that stops all resource use

questions.explanation: Sustainable development meets present needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs. It integrates environmental protection, social equity and economic viability.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What is resource depletion?

options.B: Reduction in the quantity, quality or accessibility of a resource due to overuse, degradation or contamination

questions.explanation: Resource depletion is reduction in the quantity, quality or accessibility of a resource due to overuse, degradation or contamination. Examples include groundwater decline, soil nutrient loss, forest degradation and depletion of high-grade mineral deposits.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What are the 3Rs of resource conservation?
questions.explanation: The 3Rs are Reduce, Reuse and Recycle. Expanded 5R hierarchies commonly include Refuse and Repair or Recover.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What is the difference between conservation and preservation?

options.A: Conservation allows regulated use; preservation emphasises keeping an area or resource in an undisturbed state
options.B: Conservation means no use; preservation means unlimited use
options.D: Conservation is only for forests; preservation is only for wildlife

questions.explanation: Conservation usually means careful protection and sustainable management that may allow regulated use. Preservation emphasises keeping an area or resource in an undisturbed state.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What is environmental pollution?

options.A: The introduction of substances or energy into the environment at levels or in forms that cause or threaten harmful effects

questions.explanation: Pollution is the introduction of substances or energy into the environment at levels or in forms that cause or threaten harmful effects to organisms, ecosystems, property or human well-being.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following is a major source of air pollution?
questions.explanation: Major sources of air pollution include transport, thermal power plants, industries, construction and road dust, waste and biomass burning, household solid fuels, agricultural residue burning and natural sources such as dust storms and wildfires.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following is a secondary air pollutant?
questions.explanation: Ground-level ozone is a secondary pollutant formed through sunlight-driven reactions involving NOx and VOCs.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What are primary pollutants?

options.A: Pollutants formed in the atmosphere through chemical reactions
options.B: Pollutants emitted directly, e.g. carbon monoxide, sulphur dioxide and some particulate matter

questions.explanation: Primary pollutants are emitted directly, e.g. carbon monoxide, sulphur dioxide and some particulate matter. Secondary pollutants form in the atmosphere through chemical reactions.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What is eutrophication?

options.A: Excess nutrient enrichment—especially nitrogen and phosphorus—stimulating algal and plant growth

questions.explanation: Eutrophication is excess nutrient enrichment—especially nitrogen and phosphorus—that can stimulate algal and plant growth. Decomposition of the resulting biomass consumes dissolved oxygen, causing hypoxia, fish kills and ecosystem change.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What is Biochemical Oxygen Demand (BOD)?

options.A: Oxygen consumed by micro-organisms while decomposing biodegradable organic matter in a water sample under specified test conditions
options.B: Oxygen required to chemically oxidise all substances

questions.explanation: BOD is the oxygen consumed by micro-organisms while decomposing biodegradable organic matter in a water sample under specified test conditions, commonly BOD at 20°C.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: High BOD in water generally indicates:
questions.explanation: High BOD often indicates substantial biodegradable organic pollution and potential oxygen depletion.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Differentiate BOD and COD.

options.A: BOD estimates oxygen used by biological oxidation of biodegradable matter; COD estimates oxygen equivalent required to chemically oxidise oxidisable substances
options.B: BOD is measured more quickly than COD
options.C: COD is always lower than BOD

questions.explanation: BOD estimates oxygen used by biological oxidation of biodegradable matter over a defined period. COD estimates oxygen equivalent required to chemically oxidise oxidisable substances and is usually measured more quickly; COD is generally higher than BOD for the same sample.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What is Dissolved Oxygen (DO) and why is it important?

options.A: Oxygen dissolved in water and available to aquatic organisms; low DO can stress or kill fish and invertebrates

questions.explanation: DO is oxygen dissolved in water and available to aquatic organisms. Low DO can stress or kill fish and invertebrates; temperature, salinity, turbulence, photosynthesis and organic pollution influence DO.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What causes soil pollution?
questions.explanation: Soil pollution is caused by excess pesticides and fertilisers, industrial chemicals, heavy metals, mining waste, oil leaks, landfill leachate, plastics, sewage sludge and improper hazardous-waste disposal.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What is noise pollution?

options.A: Unwanted or excessive sound that adversely affects health or the environment

questions.explanation: Noise pollution is unwanted or excessive sound that adversely affects health or the environment. Sources include road, rail and air traffic, construction, industries, loudspeakers and generators.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What is thermal pollution?

options.A: An undesirable change in water or air temperature, often from heated industrial or power-station discharges

questions.explanation: Thermal pollution is an undesirable change in water or air temperature, often from heated industrial or power-station discharges, which can reduce dissolved oxygen and alter aquatic ecology.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What is radioactive pollution?

options.A: The release or presence of radionuclides above safe levels

questions.explanation: Radioactive pollution is the release or presence of radionuclides above safe levels, from accidents, improper waste handling, mining or other sources.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What are microplastics?

options.A: Plastic particles generally smaller than 5 mm

questions.explanation: Microplastics are generally plastic particles smaller than 5 mm; they can be ingested by organisms, transport chemicals and persist in ecosystems.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What is India's National AQI category for the index range 0–50?
questions.explanation: The six AQI categories are Good (0–50), Satisfactory (51–100), Moderately Polluted (101–200), Poor (201–300), Very Poor (301–400) and Severe (401–500).

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What is India's National AQI category for the index range 301–400?
questions.explanation: Very Poor corresponds to the AQI range 301–400.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What is the AQI range for the 'Severe' category in India?
questions.explanation: Severe corresponds to the AQI range 401–500.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What is water quality?

options.A: Physical, chemical and biological characteristics relative to a use or ecosystem requirement

questions.explanation: Water quality describes physical, chemical and biological characteristics relative to a use or ecosystem requirement. Common indicators include pH, turbidity, temperature, conductivity, dissolved oxygen, BOD, COD, nutrients, pathogens and toxic chemicals.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What is solid waste management?

options.A: The systematic segregation, collection, storage, transport, processing, recovery and safe disposal of solid waste

questions.explanation: Solid waste management is the systematic segregation, collection, storage, transport, processing, recovery and safe disposal of solid waste. Source segregation, material recovery, composting, biomethanation, recycling and engineered landfills are key components.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What is e-waste?

options.A: Discarded electrical and electronic equipment and their components

questions.explanation: E-waste is discarded electrical and electronic equipment and their components. It may contain valuable recoverable materials as well as hazardous substances; collection, authorised dismantling, recycling and producer responsibility are important.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What is biomedical waste?

options.A: Waste generated during diagnosis, treatment or immunisation of humans or animals, or related research and production/testing of biologicals

questions.explanation: Biomedical waste is waste generated during diagnosis, treatment or immunisation of humans or animals, or related research and production/testing of biologicals. It requires segregation, colour-coded handling, treatment and disposal under applicable rules.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What is hazardous waste?

options.A: Waste whose physical, chemical, biological or other properties can cause danger to health or the environment

questions.explanation: Hazardous waste is waste whose physical, chemical, biological or other properties can cause danger to health or the environment. Examples include certain toxic, corrosive, flammable or reactive industrial wastes and contaminated residues.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What are the typical stages of sewage treatment?

options.A: Preliminary screening and grit removal; primary settling; secondary biological treatment; and where required, tertiary treatment and disinfection

questions.explanation: Typical sewage treatment includes preliminary screening and grit removal; primary settling; secondary biological treatment such as activated sludge or trickling filters; and, where required, tertiary treatment and disinfection. Sludge is separately treated and safely managed.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What is an Effluent Treatment Plant (ETP)?

options.A: A plant that treats industrial wastewater using processes such as screening, equalisation, pH correction, coagulation/flocculation, sedimentation, biological treatment, filtration, adsorption, membrane treatment and disinfection
options.B: A plant that treats solid waste
options.D: A plant that treats air pollution

questions.explanation: An effluent treatment plant (ETP) treats industrial wastewater. Processes may include screening, equalisation, pH correction, coagulation/flocculation, sedimentation, biological treatment, filtration, adsorption, membrane treatment and disinfection, depending on pollutants and discharge standards.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: How can air pollution be controlled?

options.A: Cleaner fuels and energy, public transport, emission standards, industrial scrubbers and filters, dust suppression

questions.explanation: Air pollution control measures include cleaner fuels and energy, public transport, emission standards, industrial scrubbers and filters, dust suppression, better construction practices, clean household energy, waste-burning prevention, green infrastructure and continuous monitoring.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What is the waste-management hierarchy?

options.A: Prevention and reduction first, then reuse, recycling and recovery; treatment follows where needed; disposal is the least preferred option

questions.explanation: The waste-management hierarchy places prevention and reduction first, then reuse, recycling and recovery; treatment follows where needed, while disposal is the least preferred option. Safe disposal remains necessary for residual and hazardous fractions.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.topic: Climate Change and Global Environmental Issues
questions.chapter: 3.10.6 Climate Change and Global Environmental Issues
questions.question: What is the greenhouse effect?

options.A: Certain atmospheric gases absorb and re-emit outgoing long-wave infrared radiation, warming the lower atmosphere and surface
options.B: The reflection of sunlight by clouds
options.C: The absorption of UV radiation by ozone
options.D: The cooling of the Earth's surface

questions.explanation: Certain atmospheric gases absorb and re-emit outgoing long-wave infrared radiation, warming the lower atmosphere and surface. The natural greenhouse effect makes Earth habitable; human emissions enhance it and cause additional warming.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.topic: Climate Change and Global Environmental Issues
questions.chapter: 3.10.6 Climate Change and Global Environmental Issues
questions.question: Differentiate the natural greenhouse effect and enhanced greenhouse effect.

options.A: The natural greenhouse effect is a normal physical process; the enhanced greenhouse effect is additional warming caused by rising greenhouse gas concentrations due mainly to human activities
options.B: Both are caused only by human activities
options.C: The natural greenhouse effect is caused by human activities; the enhanced is natural

questions.explanation: The natural greenhouse effect is a normal physical process. The enhanced greenhouse effect is the additional warming caused by rising concentrations of greenhouse gases due mainly to human activities such as fossil-fuel combustion, deforestation, agriculture and industrial processes.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.topic: Climate Change and Global Environmental Issues
questions.chapter: 3.10.6 Climate Change and Global Environmental Issues
questions.question: Which of the following is a major greenhouse gas?
questions.explanation: Major greenhouse gases include water vapour, carbon dioxide (CO2), methane (CH4), nitrous oxide (N2O), ozone and fluorinated gases including CFCs, HFCs, PFCs, SF6 and NF3.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.topic: Climate Change and Global Environmental Issues
questions.chapter: 3.10.6 Climate Change and Global Environmental Issues
questions.question: What are the main human sources of carbon dioxide?

options.A: Fossil-fuel combustion, cement production and land-use change

questions.explanation: CO2 sources: fossil-fuel combustion, cement production and land-use change. CH4: livestock, rice cultivation, fossil-fuel systems, landfills and wetlands (natural). N2O: agricultural soils and nitrogen fertilisers, manure, industry and combustion.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.topic: Climate Change and Global Environmental Issues
questions.chapter: 3.10.6 Climate Change and Global Environmental Issues
questions.question: What are the main human sources of methane (CH4)?

options.A: Livestock, rice cultivation, fossil-fuel systems and landfills

questions.explanation: CH4 sources include livestock, rice cultivation, fossil-fuel systems, landfills and wetlands (natural).

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.topic: Climate Change and Global Environmental Issues
questions.chapter: 3.10.6 Climate Change and Global Environmental Issues
questions.question: What are the main human sources of nitrous oxide (N2O)?

options.A: Agricultural soils and nitrogen fertilisers, manure, industry and combustion

questions.explanation: N2O sources include agricultural soils and nitrogen fertilisers, manure, industry and combustion.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.topic: Climate Change and Global Environmental Issues
questions.chapter: 3.10.6 Climate Change and Global Environmental Issues
questions.question: What are Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs)?

options.A: Synthetic compounds once widely used in refrigeration, aerosols and foam production that destroy stratospheric ozone and are also potent greenhouse gases
options.C: Compounds that only cause global warming
options.D: Compounds that only cause acid rain

questions.explanation: CFCs are synthetic compounds once widely used in refrigeration, aerosols and foam production. In the stratosphere, chlorine released from them catalytically destroys ozone. They are also potent greenhouse gases; their production and consumption have been phased out for most controlled uses under the Montreal Protocol.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.topic: Climate Change and Global Environmental Issues
questions.chapter: 3.10.6 Climate Change and Global Environmental Issues
questions.question: What is ozone depletion?

options.A: The thinning of the stratospheric ozone layer caused mainly by ozone-depleting substances that release chlorine or bromine in the stratosphere
options.B: The increase of ozone at ground level
options.C: The formation of ozone in the troposphere
options.D: The absorption of ozone by plants

questions.explanation: Stratospheric ozone depletion is the thinning of the ozone layer caused mainly by ozone-depleting substances that release chlorine or bromine in the stratosphere. It increases harmful UV-B reaching the surface. The ozone hole is most pronounced seasonally over Antarctica.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.topic: Climate Change and Global Environmental Issues
questions.chapter: 3.10.6 Climate Change and Global Environmental Issues
questions.question: Differentiate stratospheric ozone and ground-level ozone.

options.A: Stratospheric ozone absorbs harmful ultraviolet radiation and is protective; ground-level ozone is a secondary air pollutant and respiratory irritant
options.C: Stratospheric ozone is harmful; ground-level ozone is protective

questions.explanation: Stratospheric ozone absorbs harmful ultraviolet radiation and is protective. Ground-level ozone is a secondary air pollutant and respiratory irritant formed by photochemical reactions involving nitrogen oxides and volatile organic compounds.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.topic: Climate Change and Global Environmental Issues
questions.chapter: 3.10.6 Climate Change and Global Environmental Issues
questions.question: What is acid rain?

options.A: Precipitation or deposition made unusually acidic mainly by sulphuric and nitric acids formed from SO2 and NOx emissions

questions.explanation: Acid rain is precipitation or deposition made unusually acidic mainly by sulphuric and nitric acids formed from SO2 and NOx emissions. It can acidify lakes and soils, damage vegetation and corrode buildings. The term also includes dry deposition of acidic gases and particles.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.topic: Climate Change and Global Environmental Issues
questions.chapter: 3.10.6 Climate Change and Global Environmental Issues
questions.question: What is climate change?

options.A: Long-term change in the mean state or variability of climate, typically over decades or longer

questions.explanation: Climate change is long-term change in the mean state or variability of climate, typically over decades or longer. Modern rapid global warming is primarily driven by human-caused greenhouse-gas emissions; natural variability also affects regional and short-term patterns.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.topic: Climate Change and Global Environmental Issues
questions.chapter: 3.10.6 Climate Change and Global Environmental Issues
questions.question: What are the major observed and projected impacts of climate change?

options.A: Rising average temperatures, more frequent/intense heat extremes, changing precipitation
options.B: Glacier and ice-sheet loss, sea-level rise, ocean warming and acidification
options.C: Shifts in ecosystems and risks to food, water, health, infrastructure and livelihoods

questions.explanation: Impacts include rising average temperatures, more frequent/intense heat extremes, changing precipitation, glacier and ice-sheet loss, sea-level rise, ocean warming and acidification, shifts in ecosystems and risks to food, water, health, infrastructure and livelihoods.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.topic: Climate Change and Global Environmental Issues
questions.chapter: 3.10.6 Climate Change and Global Environmental Issues
questions.question: Why are glaciers melting and why does it matter?

options.A: Warming air and oceans increase glacier mass loss; glacier retreat affects seasonal river flows, water storage, glacial-lake outburst flood risk and mountain ecosystems
options.B: Glaciers are melting due to volcanic activity only
options.D: Glaciers are growing due to cooling

questions.explanation: Warming air and oceans increase glacier mass loss. Glacier retreat affects seasonal river flows, water storage, glacial-lake outburst flood risk and mountain ecosystems. Individual glaciers also respond to precipitation, debris cover and local conditions.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.topic: Climate Change and Global Environmental Issues
questions.chapter: 3.10.6 Climate Change and Global Environmental Issues
questions.question: What causes sea-level rise?

options.A: Thermal expansion of warming seawater and addition of water from melting glaciers and ice sheets

questions.explanation: Thermal expansion of warming seawater and addition of water from melting glaciers and ice sheets are the major contributors. Local relative sea level also depends on land subsidence or uplift, ocean circulation and gravitational effects.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.topic: Climate Change and Global Environmental Issues
questions.chapter: 3.10.6 Climate Change and Global Environmental Issues
questions.question: What is ocean acidification?

options.A: The ocean absorbs atmospheric CO2; dissolved CO2 forms carbonic acid and lowers seawater pH while reducing carbonate-ion availability

questions.explanation: The ocean absorbs atmospheric CO2; dissolved CO2 forms carbonic acid and lowers seawater pH while reducing carbonate-ion availability. This can make shell and skeleton formation harder for corals and some shell-forming organisms.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.topic: Climate Change and Global Environmental Issues
questions.chapter: 3.10.6 Climate Change and Global Environmental Issues
questions.question: What is coral bleaching?

options.A: When corals lose or expel symbiotic algae (or their pigments) under stress, commonly elevated sea temperature

questions.explanation: Coral bleaching occurs when corals lose or expel symbiotic algae (or their pigments) under stress, commonly elevated sea temperature. Bleached corals are not necessarily dead, but prolonged stress can cause mortality and reef degradation.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.topic: Climate Change and Global Environmental Issues
questions.chapter: 3.10.6 Climate Change and Global Environmental Issues
questions.question: What is desertification?

options.A: Land degradation in arid, semi-arid and dry sub-humid areas resulting from climatic variations and human activities
options.B: The natural expansion of deserts only
options.C: The formation of new deserts only

questions.explanation: Desertification is land degradation in arid, semi-arid and dry sub-humid areas resulting from climatic variations and human activities. It is not simply the natural spread of existing deserts; causes include overgrazing, deforestation, unsustainable cultivation, water mismanagement and drought.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.topic: Climate Change and Global Environmental Issues
questions.chapter: 3.10.6 Climate Change and Global Environmental Issues
questions.question: Differentiate deforestation and forest degradation.

options.A: Deforestation is conversion of forest to another land use or long-term loss of forest cover; forest degradation is reduction in a forest's ecological quality, biomass, structure or capacity to provide services while it may remain classified as forest
options.B: Deforestation is loss of forest quality; forest degradation is complete removal of forest
options.D: Deforestation is only in tropical areas; forest degradation is only in temperate areas

questions.explanation: Deforestation is conversion of forest to another land use or long-term loss of forest cover under the applicable definition. Forest degradation is reduction in a forest's ecological quality, biomass, structure or capacity to provide services while it may remain classified as forest.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.topic: Climate Change and Global Environmental Issues
questions.chapter: 3.10.6 Climate Change and Global Environmental Issues
questions.question: What is a carbon footprint?

options.A: The total direct and indirect greenhouse-gas emissions associated with an individual, product, organisation, activity or event, usually expressed as carbon-dioxide equivalent (CO2e)
options.B: The physical footprint of a carbon atom
options.C: The amount of carbon in soil
options.D: The weight of carbon in a forest

questions.explanation: A carbon footprint is the total direct and indirect greenhouse-gas emissions associated with an individual, product, organisation, activity or event, usually expressed as carbon-dioxide equivalent (CO2e) over a defined boundary and period.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.topic: Climate Change and Global Environmental Issues
questions.chapter: 3.10.6 Climate Change and Global Environmental Issues
questions.question: What is carbon sequestration?

options.A: The capture and long-term storage of atmospheric CO2e in biological, geological or engineered reservoirs
options.B: The release of carbon into the atmosphere

questions.explanation: Carbon sequestration is the capture and long-term storage of atmospheric CO2e in biological, geological or engineered reservoirs. Examples include forest and soil carbon storage, geological storage and certain mineralisation processes.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.topic: Climate Change and Global Environmental Issues
questions.chapter: 3.10.6 Climate Change and Global Environmental Issues
questions.question: Differentiate carbon neutrality and net zero emissions.

options.A: Carbon neutrality commonly means balancing measured CO2 emissions with removals or offsets within a defined boundary; net zero greenhouse-gas emissions means reducing anthropogenic emissions as deeply as feasible and balancing remaining emissions with removals across specified gases and boundaries
options.C: Carbon neutrality covers all gases; net zero covers only CO2
options.D: Net zero is only for companies; carbon neutrality is only for countries

questions.explanation: Carbon neutrality commonly means balancing measured CO2 emissions with removals or offsets within a defined boundary. Net zero greenhouse-gas emissions means reducing anthropogenic emissions as deeply as feasible and balancing remaining emissions with removals, across specified gases and boundaries. Definitions and claims must state scope and accounting rules.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.topic: Climate Change and Global Environmental Issues
questions.chapter: 3.10.6 Climate Change and Global Environmental Issues
questions.question: What is climate resilience?

options.A: The capacity of social, ecological and economic systems to anticipate, absorb, recover from and adapt to climate-related hazards while maintaining essential functions
options.B: The ability to prevent all climate change
options.C: The ability to ignore climate impacts

questions.explanation: Climate resilience is the capacity of social, ecological and economic systems to anticipate, absorb, recover from and adapt to climate-related hazards while maintaining essential functions and the ability to transform when necessary.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.topic: Climate Change and Global Environmental Issues
questions.chapter: 3.10.6 Climate Change and Global Environmental Issues
questions.question: Which is a climate adaptation measure?
questions.explanation: Heat-action plans reduce vulnerability to heat impacts; the others are mitigation measures.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.topic: Climate Change and Global Environmental Issues
questions.chapter: 3.10.6 Climate Change and Global Environmental Issues
questions.question: Differentiate climate adaptation and mitigation.

options.A: Adaptation adjusts systems to actual or expected climate impacts; mitigation reduces greenhouse-gas sources or enhances sinks
options.B: Adaptation reduces emissions; mitigation adjusts to impacts
options.D: Adaptation is only for developed countries; mitigation is only for developing countries

questions.explanation: Adaptation adjusts systems to actual or expected climate impacts—such as heat action plans, flood-resilient infrastructure and drought-tolerant crops. Mitigation reduces greenhouse-gas sources or enhances sinks—such as renewable energy, efficiency, forest protection and methane reduction.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.topic: Climate Change and Global Environmental Issues
questions.chapter: 3.10.6 Climate Change and Global Environmental Issues
questions.question: What is the difference between weather and climate?

options.A: Weather describes short-term atmospheric conditions; climate describes long-term statistics and patterns of weather, conventionally assessed over 30-year periods
options.B: Weather is long-term; climate is short-term
options.C: Both refer to the same thing
options.D: Weather is only temperature; climate is only rainfall

questions.explanation: Weather describes short-term atmospheric conditions; climate describes long-term statistics and patterns of weather, conventionally assessed over 30-year periods, while other time windows may be used for specific analyses.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What is UNEP?

options.A: The United Nations Environment Programme, established in 1972, is the UN's leading environmental authority

questions.explanation: The United Nations Environment Programme, established in 1972, is the UN's leading environmental authority. It assesses global environmental conditions, supports environmental governance and coordinates environmental work across the UN system. Headquarters: Nairobi, Kenya.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Where is the headquarters of UNEP located?
questions.explanation: UNEP headquarters is in Nairobi, Kenya.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What is the IPCC?

options.A: The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, established in 1988 by UNEP and WMO, assesses scientific, technical and socio-economic information relevant to climate change

questions.explanation: The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, established in 1988 by UNEP and the World Meteorological Organization, assesses scientific, technical and socio-economic information relevant to climate change. It assesses evidence; it does not conduct original research or prescribe policy.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Does the IPCC conduct original research?

options.A: Yes, it conducts all original climate research
options.B: No, it assesses evidence; it does not conduct original research or prescribe policy
options.C: Yes, but only in developed countries
options.D: Yes, but only on ocean acidification

questions.explanation: The IPCC assesses evidence; it does not conduct original research or prescribe policy.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: When was the UNFCCC adopted and when did it enter into force?

options.A: Adopted in 1992 and entered into force in 1994
options.B: Adopted in 1987 and entered into force in 1989
options.C: Adopted in 1997 and entered into force in 2005
options.D: Adopted in 2015 and entered into force in 2016

questions.explanation: The United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change was adopted in 1992 and entered into force in 1994.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What is the main decision-making forum of the UNFCCC?
questions.explanation: The annual Conference of the Parties (COP) is the main decision-making forum of the UNFCCC.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: When was the Kyoto Protocol adopted and when did it enter into force?

options.A: Adopted in 1992 and in force from 1994
options.B: Adopted in 1997 and in force from 2005
options.C: Adopted in 2015 and in force from 2016
options.D: Adopted in 1987 and in force from 1989

questions.explanation: The Kyoto Protocol was adopted in 1997 and in force from 2005. It set legally binding emission-reduction targets for developed-country Parties.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which mechanisms were introduced under the Kyoto Protocol?

options.A: Emissions trading, Clean Development Mechanism and Joint Implementation

questions.explanation: The Kyoto Protocol introduced mechanisms including emissions trading, Clean Development Mechanism and Joint Implementation.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: When was the Paris Agreement adopted and when did it enter into force?

options.A: Adopted in 1992 and in force from 1994
options.B: Adopted in 1997 and in force from 2005
options.C: Adopted in 2015 and in force from 2016
options.D: Adopted in 1987 and in force from 1989

questions.explanation: The Paris Agreement was adopted in 2015 under the UNFCCC and in force from 2016.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What is the temperature goal of the Paris Agreement?

options.A: To hold the increase in global average temperature to well below 2°C above pre-industrial levels and pursue efforts to limit it to 1.5°C
options.D: To cool the Earth below pre-industrial levels

questions.explanation: The Paris Agreement aims to hold the increase in global average temperature to well below 2°C above pre-industrial levels and pursue efforts to limit it to 1.5°C.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What do parties submit under the Paris Agreement?

options.B: Binding emission targets for all countries

questions.explanation: Parties submit nationally determined contributions (NDCs) and strengthen them over time under the Paris Agreement.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: When was the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD) adopted and when did it enter into force?

options.A: Adopted in 1992 and in force from 1993
options.B: Adopted in 1971 and in force from 1975
options.C: Adopted in 1973 and in force from 1975
options.D: Adopted in 1987 and in force from 1989

questions.explanation: The CBD was adopted at the 1992 Rio Earth Summit and in force from 1993.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which framework was adopted in 2022 under the CBD?
questions.explanation: The Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework was adopted in 2022 under the CBD.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Where was the Ramsar Convention adopted and when?
questions.explanation: The Convention on Wetlands was adopted at Ramsar, Iran, on 2 February 1971 and entered into force in 1975.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: When is World Wetlands Day observed?
questions.explanation: World Wetlands Day is 2 February, marking the adoption of the Ramsar Convention.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: When was CITES adopted and when did it enter into force?

options.A: Adopted in 1973 and in force from 1975
options.B: Adopted in 1971 and in force from 1975
options.C: Adopted in 1992 and in force from 1993
options.D: Adopted in 1987 and in force from 1989

questions.explanation: CITES was adopted in 1973 and in force from 1975.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What is the purpose of CITES Appendices I, II and III?

options.A: They have different levels and mechanisms of trade control for listed species

questions.explanation: CITES Appendices I, II and III have different levels and mechanisms of trade control.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
