questions.question: When was the Montreal Protocol adopted and when did it enter into force?

options.A: Adopted in 1987 and in force from 1989
options.B: Adopted in 1992 and in force from 1994
options.C: Adopted in 1997 and in force from 2005
options.D: Adopted in 2015 and in force from 2016

questions.explanation: The Montreal Protocol was adopted in 1987 and in force from 1989 under the Vienna Convention.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What does the Montreal Protocol control?

options.A: Production and consumption of ozone-depleting substances

questions.explanation: The Montreal Protocol controls production and consumption of ozone-depleting substances.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What does the 2016 Kigali Amendment to the Montreal Protocol phase down?
questions.explanation: The 2016 Kigali Amendment phases down hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs), which are climate-warming gases but generally do not deplete ozone.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Do HFCs deplete stratospheric ozone?

options.A: Yes, they are the main ozone-depleting substances
options.B: No, they generally do not deplete ozone but can be potent greenhouse gases
options.C: Yes, but only in the Arctic
options.D: Yes, but only in the Antarctic

questions.explanation: HFCs generally do not deplete ozone but can be potent greenhouse gases. CFCs deplete ozone.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What is the Stockholm Convention concerned with?

options.A: Protecting human health and the environment from persistent organic pollutants (POPs)

questions.explanation: The Stockholm Convention is a global treaty adopted in 2001 and in force from 2004 to protect human health and the environment from persistent organic pollutants (POPs).

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What are Persistent Organic Pollutants (POPs)?

options.A: Pollutants that persist, bioaccumulate and can travel long distances

questions.explanation: POPs persist, bioaccumulate and can travel long distances.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: When was the UNCCD adopted and when did it enter into force?

options.A: Adopted in 1994 and in force from 1996
options.B: Adopted in 1992 and in force from 1994
options.C: Adopted in 1997 and in force from 2005
options.D: Adopted in 2015 and in force from 2016

questions.explanation: The UN Convention to Combat Desertification (UNCCD) was adopted in 1994 and in force from 1996.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What does the UNCCD address?

options.A: Desertification, land degradation and drought, particularly in drylands

questions.explanation: The UNCCD addresses desertification, land degradation and drought, particularly in drylands, through sustainable land management and international cooperation.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What is IUCN?

options.A: The International Union for Conservation of Nature, a membership union of government and civil-society organisations that produces scientific assessments including the Red List

questions.explanation: IUCN is a membership union of government and civil-society organisations. It provides scientific assessments, conservation standards and the IUCN Red List of Threatened Species. Headquarters: Gland, Switzerland.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Where is the headquarters of IUCN located?
questions.explanation: IUCN headquarters is in Gland, Switzerland.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What is WWF?

options.A: The World Wide Fund for Nature, an international conservation organisation

questions.explanation: The World Wide Fund for Nature is an international conservation organisation. It is not a UN agency or intergovernmental treaty.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What is the International Solar Alliance (ISA)?

options.A: An international organisation launched by India and France in 2015 to promote solar energy deployment, cooperation, investment and capacity building
options.B: A UN treaty on climate change

questions.explanation: The International Solar Alliance is an international organisation launched by India and France in 2015 to promote solar energy deployment, cooperation, investment and capacity building, particularly among solar-rich countries. Its headquarters is in India (Gurugram).

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Where is the headquarters of the International Solar Alliance located?
questions.explanation: The ISA headquarters is in Gurugram, India.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: When is World Environment Day observed?
questions.explanation: World Environment Day is observed annually on 5 June.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: When is Earth Day observed?
questions.explanation: Earth Day is observed on 22 April to mobilise public participation and awareness on environmental protection. It is a civil-society-led global observance, not a treaty.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: When is the International Day for Biological Diversity observed?
questions.explanation: The International Day for Biological Diversity is observed on 22 May, marking the adoption of the text of the Convention on Biological Diversity in 1992.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: When is World Water Day observed?
questions.explanation: World Water Day is observed on 22 March.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: When is World Wildlife Day observed?
questions.explanation: World Wildlife Day is observed on 3 March.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: When is the International Day of Forests observed?
questions.explanation: The International Day of Forests is observed on 21 March.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: When is the International Day for the Preservation of the Ozone Layer observed?
questions.explanation: The International Day for the Preservation of the Ozone Layer is observed on 16 September.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: When is World Soil Day observed?
questions.explanation: World Soil Day is observed on 5 December.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: When is World Oceans Day observed?
questions.explanation: World Oceans Day is observed on 8 June.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following is a major environmental problem in India?
questions.explanation: Major environmental problems in India include air and water pollution; solid and hazardous waste; land degradation and soil erosion; forest loss and fragmentation; biodiversity decline; groundwater stress; river and wetland degradation; coastal erosion; climate risks; and human-wildlife conflict.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What causes forest degradation in India?

options.A: Land conversion, infrastructure fragmentation and illegal felling
options.B: Unsustainable extraction, grazing pressure and fires
options.C: Invasive species, mining and climate stress

questions.explanation: Causes of forest degradation in India include land conversion, infrastructure fragmentation, illegal felling, unsustainable extraction, grazing pressure, fires, invasive species, mining and climate stress.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What are the main causes of water scarcity in India?

options.A: Uneven monsoon rainfall and over-extraction of groundwater

questions.explanation: Causes of water scarcity in India include uneven monsoon rainfall, over-extraction of groundwater, inefficient irrigation, pollution, urban demand, watershed degradation, storage and distribution gaps, and climate variability.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What causes air pollution in Indian cities?

options.B: Construction and road dust, household fuels and waste burning

questions.explanation: Air pollution in Indian cities is caused by a combination of transport, industry, power generation, construction and road dust, household fuels, waste burning, regional biomass burning and meteorology. Relative contributions differ by city and season.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What are the major sources of river pollution in India?

options.A: Untreated or partially treated municipal sewage and industrial effluent
options.C: Religious and cultural activities, erosion and low river flows

questions.explanation: Major sources of river pollution in India include untreated or partially treated municipal sewage, industrial effluent, agricultural runoff, solid waste, religious and cultural activities, erosion and low river flows.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Why is the Himalayan ecosystem vulnerable?

options.A: Steep slopes, fragile geology and tectonically active mountains

questions.explanation: Steep slopes, fragile geology, young and tectonically active mountains, intense rainfall, glaciers and snow, high biodiversity and concentrated infrastructure make the Himalayan region sensitive to landslides, floods, road construction, hydropower impacts and climate change.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Why are the Western Ghats important for conservation?

options.A: They are a global biodiversity hotspot with high endemism
options.B: They influence monsoon rainfall and feed major peninsular rivers

questions.explanation: The Western Ghats are a global biodiversity hotspot, contain high endemism, influence monsoon rainfall and feed major peninsular rivers. Threats include habitat fragmentation, plantations and infrastructure expansion, quarrying, invasive species, fire and human-wildlife conflict.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Why are coastal ecosystems important?

options.A: Mangroves, estuaries, coral reefs, seagrass beds and wetlands support fisheries and biodiversity
options.B: They store carbon and buffer waves, storms and erosion

questions.explanation: Coastal ecosystems support fisheries and biodiversity, store carbon and buffer waves, storms and erosion. They are threatened by reclamation, pollution, ports, aquaculture, sand mining and sea-level rise.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What is the importance of mangroves in India?

options.A: They stabilise shorelines, trap sediments and store carbon
options.B: They provide nursery habitat for fish and crustaceans

questions.explanation: Mangroves are salt-tolerant coastal forests that stabilise shorelines, trap sediments, store carbon, provide nursery habitat for fish and crustaceans and reduce some storm impacts. Their protection is important along the east and west coasts, including the Sundarbans, Gujarat and Andaman-Nicobar Islands.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What are wetlands?

options.A: Ecosystems where water is the primary factor controlling the environment and associated plant and animal life

questions.explanation: Wetlands are ecosystems where water is the primary factor controlling the environment and associated plant and animal life. They store and filter water, recharge groundwater, reduce floods, support fisheries and migratory birds, and store carbon in some settings.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What is a Ramsar Site?

options.A: A wetland designated as a Wetland of International Importance under the Ramsar Convention

questions.explanation: A Ramsar Site is a wetland designated as a Wetland of International Importance under the Ramsar Convention. Designation recognises international importance and commits the country to conservation and wise use; it does not automatically mean the site is a national park.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: How many Ramsar Sites did India have as of 15 October 2026?
questions.explanation: India had 103 Ramsar Sites as of 15 October 2026, following the addition of Sukhna Wetland (Chandigarh) and Sauj Jheel (Uttar Pradesh). The count is time-sensitive and should be checked against the Ramsar Secretariat.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which were India's first Ramsar Sites?

options.A: Chilika Lake in Odisha and Keoladeo National Park in Rajasthan

questions.explanation: Chilika Lake in Odisha and Keoladeo National Park in Rajasthan were designated on 1 October 1981 as India's first Ramsar Sites.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What is the Montreux Record?

options.A: A register of Ramsar Sites where changes in ecological character have occurred, are occurring or are likely to occur
options.B: A list of all threatened species
options.C: A list of all national parks

questions.explanation: The Montreux Record is a register of Ramsar Sites where changes in ecological character have occurred, are occurring or are likely to occur as a result of technological development, pollution or other human interference. It is a monitoring mechanism, not a list of all threatened wetlands.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following is a category of protected area under the Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972?
questions.explanation: Main categories of protected areas in India include national parks, wildlife sanctuaries, conservation reserves and community reserves under the Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What is Project Tiger?

options.A: A centrally sponsored conservation programme launched in 1973 to maintain viable tiger populations in their natural habitats
options.B: A project to build tiger zoos
options.C: A project to increase tiger trade
options.D: A project to remove tigers from forests

questions.explanation: Project Tiger is a centrally sponsored conservation programme launched in 1973 to maintain viable tiger populations in their natural habitats, protect ecosystems and support landscape-level conservation. National Tiger Conservation Authority (NTCA) provides statutory oversight.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What is Project Elephant?

options.A: A centrally sponsored scheme launched in 1992 to protect elephants, their habitats and corridors, reduce human-elephant conflict and support welfare of captive elephants
options.B: A project to increase elephant trade
options.C: A project to build elephant zoos
options.D: A project to remove elephants from forests

questions.explanation: Project Elephant is a centrally sponsored scheme launched in 1992 to protect elephants, their habitats and corridors, reduce human-elephant conflict and support welfare of captive elephants. Elephant reserves are identified under the programme.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What is the role of the National Green Tribunal (NGT)?

options.A: It provides specialised adjudication of environmental disputes, including substantial questions relating to the environment and enforcement of legal rights

questions.explanation: The NGT, established under the National Green Tribunal Act, 2010, provides specialised adjudication of environmental disputes, including substantial questions relating to the environment and enforcement of legal rights, and relief and compensation for environmental damage.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What is the role of the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB)?

options.A: It advises the Central Government, coordinates State Pollution Control Boards, sets or recommends standards, monitors pollution and supports enforcement

questions.explanation: CPCB is a statutory body constituted under the Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974. It advises the Central Government, coordinates State Pollution Control Boards, sets or recommends standards, monitors pollution and supports enforcement under relevant laws.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which body implements pollution-control laws at the state level in Karnataka?
questions.explanation: In Karnataka, the Karnataka State Pollution Control Board performs the role of implementing pollution-control laws at state level.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: When was the Wild Life (Protection) Act enacted in India?
questions.explanation: The Wild Life (Protection) Act was enacted in 1972.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: When was the Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act enacted?
questions.explanation: The Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act was enacted in 1974.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: When was the Forest (Conservation) Act enacted in India?
questions.explanation: The Forest (Conservation) Act was enacted in 1980.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: When was the Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act enacted?
questions.explanation: The Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act was enacted in 1981.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: When was the Environment (Protection) Act enacted in India?
questions.explanation: The Environment (Protection) Act is Act 29 of 1986.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What is the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986?

options.A: An umbrella legislation enacted after the 1972 Stockholm Conference to provide for protection and improvement of the environment
options.D: A law only about water pollution

questions.explanation: The Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 is an umbrella legislation enacted after the 1972 Stockholm Conference to provide for protection and improvement of the environment. It empowers the Central Government to take measures, prescribe standards and regulate activities and hazardous substances.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What is the Biological Diversity Act, 2002?

options.A: It gives effect to India's CBD obligations through conservation, sustainable use and fair and equitable benefit-sharing

questions.explanation: The Biological Diversity Act, 2002 gives effect to India's CBD obligations through conservation of biological diversity, sustainable use and fair and equitable benefit-sharing. Its institutional framework includes the National Biodiversity Authority, State Biodiversity Boards and Biodiversity Management Committees.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What is the EIA process?

options.A: Environmental Impact Assessment identifies and evaluates likely environmental effects of a proposed project before key decisions

questions.explanation: Environmental Impact Assessment identifies and evaluates likely environmental effects of a proposed project before key decisions. Under India's EIA Notification, 2006, applicable projects undergo screening, scoping, public consultation where required, appraisal and environmental clearance, with monitoring and compliance conditions.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What is the Coastal Regulation Zone (CRZ) framework?

options.A: A framework under the Environment (Protection) Act that regulates specified activities along India's coastal stretches to protect coastal ecosystems and livelihoods
options.C: A framework for managing wildlife trade
options.D: A framework for managing air pollution

questions.explanation: The CRZ framework under the Environment (Protection) Act regulates specified activities along India's coastal stretches to protect coastal ecosystems and livelihoods while managing development.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following is an important national environmental programme in India?
questions.explanation: Important national environmental programmes include the National Action Plan on Climate Change and its missions; National Clean Air Programme; Namami Gange; National Plan for Conservation of Aquatic Ecosystems; Green India Mission; CAMPA-funded afforestation and restoration; Project Tiger; Project Elephant; and MISHTI for mangrove restoration.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following is a major environmental problem of Karnataka?

options.A: Forest and habitat fragmentation and pressure on the Western Ghats
options.B: River and lake pollution and groundwater depletion

questions.explanation: Major environmental problems of Karnataka include forest and habitat fragmentation, pressure on the Western Ghats, river and lake pollution, groundwater depletion, mining-related impacts, drought and floods, forest fires, soil erosion, coastal erosion, urban air pollution, solid waste, human-wildlife conflict and invasive species.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Why is Western Ghats conservation important to Karnataka?

options.A: The Ghats contain high biodiversity and endemism
options.B: They regulate catchments and rainfall and feed major rivers

questions.explanation: The Ghats contain high biodiversity and endemism, regulate catchments and rainfall, and feed major rivers. Conservation priorities include maintaining contiguous native forests, protecting headwaters, regulating ecologically damaging land conversion and quarrying, restoring degraded habitats and supporting local livelihoods.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What causes river pollution in Karnataka?

options.A: Untreated municipal sewage and industrial discharges
options.C: Sand extraction and reduced dilution during low flows

questions.explanation: Causes of river pollution in Karnataka include untreated municipal sewage, industrial discharges, agricultural runoff, solid waste, sand extraction and reduced dilution during low flows. Major river systems include the Cauvery, Krishna, Tungabhadra, Sharavathi, Kali and their tributaries.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What are common causes of lake pollution in Karnataka, especially in Bengaluru?
questions.explanation: Common causes of lake pollution in Karnataka, especially in Bengaluru, include untreated sewage, nutrient-rich inflows, encroachment, solid waste, construction debris, stormwater contamination and loss of natural wetlands. Eutrophication can produce algal blooms, odour and low dissolved oxygen.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Why is groundwater depletion a concern in Karnataka?

options.A: Dependence on borewells and irregular monsoon recharge
options.C: Hard-rock aquifers with limited storage and uneven distribution

questions.explanation: Groundwater depletion in Karnataka is caused by dependence on borewells, irregular monsoon recharge, intensive irrigation, urban demand, hard-rock aquifers with limited storage and uneven distribution. Recharge structures, watershed protection, demand management and efficient irrigation are important.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What are the environmental impacts of mining in Karnataka?

options.A: Land disturbance and removal of vegetation and topsoil
options.B: Dust, noise, waste dumps and altered drainage
options.C: Sedimentation, contamination risks and habitat fragmentation

questions.explanation: Environmental impacts of mining in Karnataka include land disturbance, removal of vegetation and topsoil, dust, noise, waste dumps, altered drainage, sedimentation, contamination risks and habitat fragmentation.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: How do droughts affect Karnataka?

options.A: Reduce crop yields and drinking-water availability
options.B: Reduce reservoir inflows and soil moisture

questions.explanation: Drought reduces crop yields, drinking-water availability, reservoir inflows, soil moisture and rural incomes. Vulnerability is high in parts of the northern and interior districts with variable rainfall.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Why does Karnataka experience floods?

options.A: Intense monsoon rainfall and saturated catchments
options.C: Urban encroachment on lakes and drains and inadequate stormwater systems

questions.explanation: Floods in Karnataka are caused by intense monsoon rainfall, saturated catchments, river overflow, reservoir releases, urban encroachment on lakes and drains, inadequate stormwater systems and coastal rainfall. Risk is not uniform across the state.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What causes forest fires in Karnataka?

options.A: Dry-season fuel accumulation and high temperatures

questions.explanation: Forest fires in Karnataka are caused by dry-season fuel accumulation, high temperatures, drought, lightning and human ignition—intentional or accidental. Prevention includes early warning, fuel management, fire lines where appropriate, community participation and rapid response.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What causes soil erosion in Karnataka?

options.A: Loss of vegetation and cultivation on slopes

questions.explanation: Soil erosion in Karnataka is caused by loss of vegetation, cultivation on slopes, intense monsoon runoff, overgrazing, quarrying and poor watershed management. Contour bunding, terracing, vegetative barriers, check dams and restoring native cover can reduce erosion.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What causes coastal erosion in Karnataka?

options.A: Wave and current action, storms and sea-level rise
options.B: Sediment imbalance caused by dams and coastal structures
options.C: Sand extraction and poorly planned development

questions.explanation: Coastal erosion in Karnataka is caused by wave and current action, storms, sea-level rise, sediment imbalance caused by dams and coastal structures, sand extraction and poorly planned development.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What are the major urban air-pollution sources in Karnataka?

options.B: Construction and road dust, industrial and power emissions
options.C: Diesel generators, waste burning and regional biomass burning

questions.explanation: Major urban air-pollution sources in Karnataka include road transport, traffic congestion, construction and road dust, industrial and power emissions, diesel generators, waste burning and regional biomass burning. Bengaluru's air quality varies with location, season and meteorology.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What are the key elements of effective waste management in Karnataka's cities?

options.A: Segregation at source and reliable collection
options.B: Decentralised wet-waste processing and dry-waste recovery
options.C: Safe handling of domestic hazardous and sanitary waste and scientific treatment of residual waste

questions.explanation: Key elements include segregation at source, reliable collection, decentralised wet-waste processing, dry-waste recovery, safe handling of domestic hazardous and sanitary waste, scientific treatment of residual waste, legacy dump remediation and enforcement of producer-responsibility systems.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What is human-wildlife conflict?

options.A: When wildlife and people compete for space or resources, causing harm to people, crops, livestock, property or animals
options.C: When wildlife is kept in zoos

questions.explanation: Human-wildlife conflict occurs when wildlife and people compete for space or resources, causing harm to people, crops, livestock, property or animals. In Karnataka, elephant and leopard interactions are prominent in some landscapes.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What are wildlife corridors?

options.A: Areas of habitat or landscape connectivity that allow animals to move between habitat patches

questions.explanation: Wildlife corridors are areas of habitat or landscape connectivity that allow animals to move between habitat patches for feeding, breeding, dispersal and gene flow. Corridors are especially important for wide-ranging species such as elephants and tigers.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following is a major protected area in Karnataka?
questions.explanation: Important protected areas in Karnataka include Bandipur, Nagarahole (Rajiv Gandhi), Bannerghatta, Anshi/Kali, Kudremukh and other national parks and wildlife sanctuaries.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following are Karnataka's tiger reserves?
questions.explanation: Major notified tiger reserves include Bandipur, Bhadra, Kali and Nagarahole. Tiger-reserve boundaries and counts can change through notifications; use the latest NTCA and Karnataka Forest Department records.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What is the Nilgiri Biosphere Reserve and how is Karnataka connected to it?

options.A: It is a UNESCO MAB-designated biosphere reserve (1986) spanning Karnataka, Kerala and Tamil Nadu; Karnataka's Bandipur and Nagarahole landscapes form important parts of this larger ecological region
options.B: It is a national park only in Karnataka
options.C: It is a Ramsar site in Karnataka
options.D: It is a tiger reserve only in Kerala

questions.explanation: The Nilgiri Biosphere Reserve, designated under UNESCO's Man and the Biosphere Programme in 1986, spans parts of Karnataka, Kerala and Tamil Nadu. Karnataka's Bandipur and Nagarahole landscapes form important parts of this larger ecological region.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: How many Ramsar sites did Karnataka have as of the current 2026 reference?
questions.explanation: Karnataka's Ramsar sites as of the current 2026 reference include Ranganathittu Bird Sanctuary, Aghanashini Estuary, Ankasamudra Bird Conservation Reserve and Magadi Kere Conservation Reserve. The state total is four in the 21 October 2026 state-wise Ramsar tally.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which Karnataka Ramsar site is an estuary?
questions.explanation: Aghanashini Estuary is a coastal wetland in Karnataka.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Why is Aghanashini Estuary ecologically important?

options.A: It is a west-coast estuarine system in Uttara Kannada district with mangroves, mudflats, fisheries, shellfish resources and bird habitats

questions.explanation: Aghanashini Estuary is a west-coast estuarine system in Uttara Kannada district with mangroves, mudflats, fisheries, shellfish resources and bird habitats. Its ecological and livelihood value makes integrated catchment and estuary management important.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What is the role of the Karnataka State Pollution Control Board (KSPCB)?

options.A: It implements pollution-control legislation in Karnataka, monitors air and water quality, grants statutory consents and authorisations, inspects facilities, regulates waste management and advises the state government

questions.explanation: KSPCB implements pollution-control legislation in Karnataka, monitors air and water quality, grants statutory consents and authorisations, inspects facilities, regulates waste management and advises the state government.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What state-level actions can improve Karnataka's environmental management?

options.A: Strengthen sewage and effluent treatment; protect lakes, wetlands and catchments
options.B: Enforce mining and waste rules; restore native forests and corridors
options.C: Improve public transport and dust control; expand rainwater harvesting and groundwater recharge; support community-led conservation; publish transparent monitoring data

questions.explanation: State-level actions include strengthening sewage and effluent treatment; protecting lakes, wetlands and catchments; enforcing mining and waste rules; restoring native forests and corridors; improving public transport and dust control; expanding rainwater harvesting and groundwater recharge; supporting community-led conservation; and publishing transparent monitoring data.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What is the difference between a national park, tiger reserve, biosphere reserve and Ramsar site in Karnataka?

options.A: A national park is a statutory protected area under wildlife law; a tiger reserve is a landscape notified under the tiger-conservation framework; a biosphere reserve is a UNESCO MAB designation; a Ramsar site is a wetland of international importance under the Wetlands Convention
options.C: A national park is a Ramsar site; a tiger reserve is a biosphere reserve
options.D: A Ramsar site is a national park; a biosphere reserve is a tiger reserve

questions.explanation: A national park is a statutory protected area under wildlife law; a tiger reserve is a landscape notified under the tiger-conservation framework; a biosphere reserve is a UNESCO MAB designation with zonation and sustainable-development goals; a Ramsar site is a wetland of international importance under the Wetlands Convention. One location may carry more than one designation.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What is the key distinction between environment and ecosystem?

options.A: Environment is the total surrounding conditions; ecosystem is a functional interacting system of organisms and abiotic factors
options.B: Environment is a functional system; ecosystem is the total surrounding conditions
options.D: Environment refers only to biotic factors; ecosystem refers only to abiotic factors

questions.explanation: Environment is the total surrounding conditions; ecosystem is a functional interacting system of organisms and abiotic factors.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What is the key distinction between a food chain and a food web?

options.A: Food chain is a linear feeding pathway; food web is an interconnected feeding network
options.B: Food chain is a network; food web is linear
options.D: Food chain refers to energy; food web refers to nutrients

questions.explanation: A food chain is a linear feeding pathway; a food web is an interconnected feeding network.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What is the key distinction between energy flow and nutrient cycle?

options.A: Energy flows one way and dissipates; matter is recycled
options.B: Energy is recycled; matter flows one way

questions.explanation: Energy flows one way and dissipates; matter (nutrients) is recycled.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What is the key distinction between primary succession and secondary succession?

options.A: No developed soil at start versus soil/biological legacies remain
options.B: Primary has soil; secondary has no soil

questions.explanation: Primary succession starts without developed soil; secondary succession occurs where soil or biological legacies remain.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What is the key distinction between in-situ and ex-situ conservation?

options.A: Conservation in natural habitat versus outside natural habitat
options.B: Conservation outside natural habitat versus in natural habitat

questions.explanation: In-situ conservation is in natural habitat; ex-situ conservation is outside natural habitat.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What is the key distinction between endemic and invasive alien species?

options.A: Restricted native range versus introduced non-native species causing harm

questions.explanation: Endemic species are restricted native species; invasive alien species are introduced non-native species causing harm.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What is the key distinction between endangered and extinct?

options.A: High extinction risk versus no surviving individuals
options.B: No surviving individuals versus high extinction risk

questions.explanation: Endangered means high extinction risk; extinct means no surviving individuals.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What is the key distinction between adaptation and mitigation?

options.A: Adjust to climate impacts versus reduce emissions or enhance sinks
options.B: Reduce emissions versus adjust to climate impacts
options.D: Both mean adjusting to climate impacts

questions.explanation: Adaptation means adjusting to climate impacts; mitigation means reducing emissions or enhancing sinks.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What is the key distinction between ozone depletion and global warming?

options.A: Stratospheric ozone loss versus enhanced greenhouse warming; distinct mechanisms
options.B: Both are caused by CFCs only
options.C: Both are caused by CO2 only

questions.explanation: Ozone depletion is stratospheric ozone loss; global warming is enhanced greenhouse warming. They have distinct mechanisms.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What is the key distinction between BOD and COD?

options.A: Biological oxygen demand versus chemically oxidisable load
options.B: Chemically oxidisable load versus biological oxygen demand
options.D: BOD measures air pollution; COD measures water pollution

questions.explanation: BOD is biological oxygen demand; COD is chemical oxygen demand (chemically oxidisable load).

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What is the key distinction between a national park and a Ramsar site?

options.A: Statutory terrestrial/wildlife protected area versus internationally recognised wetland designation
options.B: Internationally recognised wetland designation versus statutory protected area

questions.explanation: A national park is a statutory terrestrial/wildlife protected area; a Ramsar site is an internationally recognised wetland designation.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: When is World Wetlands Day observed?
questions.explanation: World Wetlands Day is observed on 2 February, marking the adoption of the Ramsar Convention in 1971.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: When was UNEP established?
questions.explanation: UNEP was established in 1972.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: When was the IPCC established?
questions.explanation: The IPCC was established in 1988.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: When was the National Green Tribunal Act enacted in India?
questions.explanation: The National Green Tribunal Act was enacted in 2010.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following statements about energy in ecosystems is correct?

options.A: Energy is recycled in ecosystems; nutrients are not cycled
options.B: Energy is not recycled in ecosystems; nutrients are cycled
options.C: Both energy and nutrients are recycled
options.D: Both energy and nutrients are not recycled

questions.explanation: Energy is not recycled in ecosystems; nutrients are cycled. This is a common examination trap.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following statements about the 10% energy-transfer rule is correct?

options.A: It is an exact law for every chain
options.B: It is an approximate ecological generalisation, not an exact law for every chain
options.C: It applies only to aquatic ecosystems
options.D: It states that 90% of energy is transferred

questions.explanation: The 10% energy-transfer rule is an approximate ecological generalisation, not an exact law for every chain.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following statements about CFCs and HFCs is correct?

options.A: CFCs deplete ozone; HFCs generally do not deplete ozone but can be potent greenhouse gases
options.B: CFCs do not deplete ozone; HFCs deplete ozone

questions.explanation: CFCs deplete ozone; HFCs generally do not deplete ozone but can be potent greenhouse gases.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following statements about the Paris Agreement and Kyoto Protocol is correct?

options.A: The Paris Agreement is based on nationally determined contributions (NDCs); the Kyoto Protocol used binding targets for developed-country Parties in commitment periods
options.B: The Paris Agreement uses binding targets for all countries; the Kyoto Protocol uses NDCs
options.D: Both use only binding targets for developing countries

questions.explanation: The Paris Agreement is based on NDCs; the Kyoto Protocol used binding targets for developed-country Parties in commitment periods.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following statements about Ramsar designation is correct?

options.A: Ramsar designation automatically makes a wetland a national park
options.B: Ramsar designation does not automatically make a wetland a national park
options.C: Ramsar designation is the same as a tiger reserve
options.D: Ramsar designation is the same as a biosphere reserve

questions.explanation: A Ramsar designation does not automatically make a wetland a national park.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following statements about alien species is correct?

options.B: Alien species are not automatically invasive; harm or likely harm is central to the definition

questions.explanation: Alien species are not automatically invasive; harm or likely harm is central to the definition.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following statements about a biosphere reserve is correct?

options.A: A biosphere reserve is a UNESCO programme designation; statutory protection comes from the applicable national/state legal categories
options.B: A biosphere reserve is a statutory national park
options.C: A biosphere reserve is a Ramsar site
options.D: A biosphere reserve is a tiger reserve

questions.explanation: A biosphere reserve is a UNESCO programme designation; statutory protection comes from the applicable national/state legal categories.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following statements about a biodiversity hotspot is correct?

options.A: A biodiversity hotspot is synonymous with a protected area
options.B: A biodiversity hotspot is not synonymous with a protected area; hotspot criteria include plant endemism and habitat loss
options.C: A biodiversity hotspot is a Ramsar site
options.D: A biodiversity hotspot is a tiger reserve

questions.explanation: A biodiversity hotspot is not synonymous with a protected area; hotspot criteria include plant endemism and habitat loss.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following statements about BOD is correct?

options.A: BOD is a direct measure of all pollutants
options.B: BOD is a measure of biodegradable organic pollution under specified test conditions; it is not a direct measure of all pollutants

questions.explanation: BOD is a measure of biodegradable organic pollution under specified test conditions; it is not a direct measure of all pollutants.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following statements about carbon neutrality and net zero claims is correct?

options.A: Carbon neutrality and net zero claims require a defined boundary, gases, accounting method and treatment of residual emissions
options.B: Carbon neutrality claims require no accounting
options.C: Net zero claims apply only to CO2
options.D: Carbon neutrality and net zero are the same

questions.explanation: Carbon neutrality and net zero claims require a defined boundary, gases, accounting method and treatment of residual emissions.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which sphere includes all forms of water on Earth?
questions.explanation: Hydrosphere includes oceans, rivers, groundwater, ice and water vapour.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following is an abiotic component?
questions.explanation: Temperature is a non-living physical factor.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which trophic level is occupied by green plants?
questions.explanation: Producers occupy the first trophic level.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which ecological pyramid is always upright?
questions.explanation: Energy is lost at each transfer, so the energy pyramid is always upright.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: The 10 per cent law is associated with:
questions.explanation: Raymond Lindeman described the approximate transfer of energy between trophic levels.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which process converts atmospheric nitrogen into biologically usable forms?
questions.explanation: Nitrogen fixation converts N2 to ammonia or related usable forms.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Primary succession begins on:
questions.explanation: Primary succession starts where developed soil is absent.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which is an example of ex-situ conservation?
questions.explanation: Seed banks conserve plant genetic material outside natural habitats.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which IUCN categories are collectively called threatened?
questions.explanation: Critically Endangered, Endangered and Vulnerable are threatened categories.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which Indian biodiversity hotspot includes the Nicobar Islands?
questions.explanation: The Nicobar Islands are the Indian part of the Sundaland hotspot.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: The Ramsar Convention is primarily concerned with:
questions.explanation: The Convention on Wetlands promotes conservation and wise use of wetlands.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: CITES regulates:

options.B: International trade in listed wild species

questions.explanation: CITES uses appendices and permits to regulate international wildlife trade.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: The Montreal Protocol controls:
questions.explanation: The Montreal Protocol phases out controlled ozone-depleting substances.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which is a secondary air pollutant?
questions.explanation: Ground-level ozone forms through atmospheric photochemical reactions.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: High BOD in water generally indicates:
questions.explanation: Microbial decomposition of organic matter consumes oxygen, raising BOD.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which gas is mainly responsible for acid deposition along with NOx?
questions.explanation: SO2 can be oxidised to sulphuric acid; NOx forms nitric acid.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Ocean acidification is driven mainly by:
questions.explanation: Absorbed CO2 forms carbonic acid and lowers seawater pH.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which is a climate adaptation measure?
questions.explanation: Heat-action plans reduce vulnerability to heat impacts; the others are mitigation measures.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: The Environment (Protection) Act in India was enacted in:
questions.explanation: The Environment (Protection) Act is Act 29 of 1986.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: The National Green Tribunal was established under the Act of:
questions.explanation: The National Green Tribunal Act was enacted in 2010.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which body coordinates pollution-control boards at the national level?
questions.explanation: CPCB coordinates SPCBs and performs statutory national functions.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: World Environment Day is observed on:
questions.explanation: World Environment Day is observed annually on 5 June.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which pair correctly matches an international agreement and its focus?
questions.explanation: Ramsar is the Convention on Wetlands.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which Karnataka Ramsar site is an estuary?
questions.explanation: Aghanashini Estuary is a coastal wetland in Karnataka.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following best describes a wildlife corridor?
questions.explanation: Corridors maintain movement and connectivity among wildlife habitats.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following correctly pairs a sphere with its meaning?

options.A: Lithosphere—all water in liquid, solid and vapour forms
options.B: Hydrosphere—solid outer Earth: crust and uppermost mantle

questions.explanation: The atmosphere is the envelope of gases around Earth. Lithosphere is solid Earth, hydrosphere is all water, and biosphere is the global zone of life.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following examples correctly illustrates interaction between the lithosphere and atmosphere?

options.A: Volcanic eruptions transferring material from the lithosphere to the atmosphere

questions.explanation: Volcanic eruptions transfer material from the lithosphere to the atmosphere. Plant uptake, transpiration and river transport also illustrate sphere interactions.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a function of an ecosystem?
questions.explanation: Major ecosystem functions are productivity, energy transfer, decomposition and nutrient cycling. Issuing currency is not an ecosystem function.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following correctly describes detritivores?

options.A: They chemically break down dead organic matter
options.B: They fragment dead organic matter, such as earthworms
options.C: They produce organic matter by photosynthesis

questions.explanation: Detritivores such as earthworms fragment dead organic matter; decomposers such as bacteria and fungi chemically break it down.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following is an example of an aquatic food chain?

options.B: Phytoplankton → zooplankton → small fish → large fish

questions.explanation: An aquatic food chain example is phytoplankton → zooplankton → small fish → large fish.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following statements about food webs is correct?

options.A: A food web is generally more realistic than a single food chain
options.B: A food web guarantees ecosystem stability
options.C: A food web has only one pathway
options.D: A food web is the same as a trophic level

questions.explanation: A food web is generally more realistic than a single chain because most organisms use more than one food source and may be eaten by several predators. Greater linkage can provide alternative energy pathways, though it does not guarantee stability.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Why is the pyramid of energy always upright?

options.A: Because energy increases at each trophic level
options.B: Because usable energy decreases at each transfer due to heat loss and metabolism
options.D: Because producers are always the largest organisms

questions.explanation: Pyramids of energy are always upright because usable energy decreases at each transfer; energy is lost as heat and through metabolism.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following is an example of a process that returns carbon to the atmosphere in the carbon cycle?
questions.explanation: Respiration and decomposition return carbon to air or water; photosynthesis absorbs carbon dioxide.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following is a key process in the nitrogen cycle?
questions.explanation: Key nitrogen cycle processes include nitrogen fixation, nitrification, assimilation, ammonification and denitrification.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following correctly matches a cycle with its main atmospheric form or reservoir?

options.A: Carbon—CO2 in oceans, biomass, soils and rocks
options.B: Nitrogen—N2 in atmosphere; soil and biomass pools
options.C: Oxygen—O2 in atmosphere and dissolved oxygen

questions.explanation: Carbon: CO2 in oceans, biomass, soils and rocks. Nitrogen: N2 in atmosphere; soil and biomass pools. Oxygen: O2 in atmosphere and dissolved oxygen. Water: water vapour; oceans, ice, groundwater.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following is a key process in the water cycle?
questions.explanation: Water cycle processes include evaporation, transpiration, condensation, precipitation, infiltration, runoff, sublimation and groundwater discharge.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following is an example of a lentic ecosystem?
questions.explanation: Lentic systems are standing waters such as lakes and ponds. Lotic systems are flowing waters such as rivers and streams.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following is an example of a lotic ecosystem?
questions.explanation: Lotic systems are flowing waters such as rivers and streams.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following is a supporting ecosystem service?
questions.explanation: Supporting services include soil formation, nutrient cycling and primary production. Food, freshwater and timber are provisioning services.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a criterion for a biodiversity hotspot?

options.A: At least 1,500 endemic vascular plant species
options.B: Loss of at least 70% of original natural vegetation

questions.explanation: Hotspot criteria include at least 1,500 endemic vascular plant species and loss of at least 70% of original natural vegetation. Presence of a national park is not a criterion.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following is an example of an endemic species of the Western Ghats?
questions.explanation: Examples associated with the Western Ghats include the lion-tailed macaque and Nilgiri tahr.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which IUCN Red List category indicates a species is 'Extinct in the Wild'?
questions.explanation: Extinct in the Wild is abbreviated EW. Extinct is EX, Critically Endangered is CR and Endangered is EN.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following is a major threat to biodiversity?
questions.explanation: Major threats include habitat loss, degradation and fragmentation; overexploitation; invasive alien species; pollution; climate change; illegal wildlife trade; disease and unsustainable land- and water-use change.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following is an example of a biosphere reserve?
questions.explanation: The Nilgiri Biosphere Reserve is a UNESCO MAB-designated biosphere reserve spanning Karnataka, Kerala and Tamil Nadu.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following is a major international biodiversity convention?
questions.explanation: Major international biodiversity conventions include the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD), CITES, Convention on Wetlands (Ramsar), Convention on Migratory Species (CMS/Bonn Convention) and World Heritage Convention.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following statements about renewable resources is correct?

options.B: Renewable resources are replenished naturally on human timescales if use remains within regeneration limits
options.C: Renewable resources form too slowly to be replenished
options.D: Renewable resources include coal and petroleum

questions.explanation: Renewable resources are replenished naturally on human timescales if use remains within regeneration limits. Renewable does not mean inexhaustible.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following is a non-renewable energy resource?
questions.explanation: Coal, petroleum and natural gas are non-renewable energy resources. Solar, wind and hydropower are renewable.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following is a method of soil conservation?
questions.explanation: Soil conservation methods include contour ploughing, terracing, strip cropping, cover crops, crop rotation, mulching, shelter belts, afforestation, controlled grazing, gully plugging, check dams and conservation tillage.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following is a method of water conservation?
questions.explanation: Water conservation methods include rainwater harvesting, watershed development, recharge structures, protection of tanks and wetlands, drip and sprinkler irrigation, leakage reduction, wastewater treatment and reuse, crop planning and demand management.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following is an approach to forest conservation?

options.A: Protect natural forests and prevent illegal felling and fires
options.B: Restore degraded areas with suitable native species
options.C: Maintain wildlife corridors and involve local communities

questions.explanation: Forest conservation approaches include protecting natural forests; preventing illegal felling and fires; restoring degraded areas with suitable native species; maintaining wildlife corridors; involving local communities; managing grazing and invasive species; and recognising legitimate forest rights while conserving biodiversity.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: How is wildlife conserved?

options.A: Through habitat protection and anti-poaching enforcement
options.B: Through scientific monitoring and wildlife corridors
options.C: Through conflict mitigation, captive breeding where justified, community participation and control of illegal trade

questions.explanation: Wildlife is conserved through habitat protection, anti-poaching enforcement, scientific monitoring, wildlife corridors, conflict mitigation, captive breeding where justified, community participation, control of illegal trade and landscape-level planning.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What is sustainable resource utilisation?

options.A: Using resources at rates and in ways that maintain ecological functions and future availability
options.B: Using all resources as quickly as possible
options.D: Using resources without regard for future generations

questions.explanation: Sustainable resource utilisation means using resources at rates and in ways that maintain ecological functions and future availability, minimise waste and pollution, respect social rights and distribute benefits fairly.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What is natural resource management?

options.A: Integrated planning and stewardship of land, water, forests, minerals and biodiversity

questions.explanation: Natural resource management is integrated planning and stewardship of land, water, forests, minerals and biodiversity, considering ecological limits, competing uses, local communities, governance, monitoring and long-term resilience.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What is water pollution?

options.A: Degradation of water quality that makes it harmful or unsuitable for uses or aquatic life
options.B: Only the addition of salt to water
options.C: Only the addition of heat to water
options.D: Only the addition of air to water

questions.explanation: Water pollution is degradation of water quality that makes it harmful or unsuitable for uses or aquatic life. Sources include untreated sewage, industrial effluent, agricultural runoff, oil spills, mining drainage, landfill leachate, plastics and thermal discharges.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following is a source of marine pollution?
questions.explanation: Marine pollution is caused by plastics, oil, sewage, nutrients, chemicals, heavy metals, ship waste, abandoned fishing gear and land-based runoff.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following is a source of marine pollution?
questions.explanation: Marine pollution is caused by plastics, oil, sewage, nutrients, chemicals, heavy metals, ship waste, abandoned fishing gear and land-based runoff.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following is an effect of noise pollution?
questions.explanation: Effects of noise pollution include sleep disturbance, stress, hearing damage and wildlife disruption.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following correctly describes industrial pollution?

options.A: Pollution arising from manufacturing, mining and energy production
options.B: Pollution from fertiliser and pesticide runoff
options.C: Pollution from sewage and transport emissions

questions.explanation: Industrial pollution arises from manufacturing, mining and energy production. Agricultural pollution includes fertiliser and pesticide runoff, manure and sediment; urban pollution includes sewage, transport emissions, construction dust, solid waste and stormwater runoff.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following correctly describes agricultural pollution?

options.B: Pollution including fertiliser and pesticide runoff, manure and sediment
options.C: Pollution from sewage and transport emissions

questions.explanation: Agricultural pollution includes fertiliser and pesticide runoff, manure and sediment.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following correctly describes urban pollution?

options.B: Pollution from fertiliser and pesticide runoff
options.C: Pollution including sewage, transport emissions, construction dust, solid waste and stormwater runoff

questions.explanation: Urban pollution includes sewage, transport emissions, construction dust, solid waste and stormwater runoff.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What is the National AQI category for the index range 51–100?
questions.explanation: Satisfactory corresponds to the AQI range 51–100.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What is the National AQI category for the index range 101–200?
questions.explanation: Moderately Polluted corresponds to the AQI range 101–200.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: What is the National AQI category for the index range 201–300?
questions.explanation: Poor corresponds to the AQI range 201–300.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following is a common indicator of water quality?
questions.explanation: Common water quality indicators include pH, turbidity, temperature, conductivity, dissolved oxygen, BOD, COD, nutrients, pathogens and toxic chemicals.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following is a key component of solid waste management?
questions.explanation: Source segregation, material recovery, composting, biomethanation, recycling and engineered landfills are key components of solid waste management.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.topic: Climate Change and Global Environmental Issues
questions.chapter: 3.10.6 Climate Change and Global Environmental Issues
questions.question: Which of the following is a major greenhouse gas?
questions.explanation: Major greenhouse gases include water vapour, carbon dioxide (CO2), methane (CH4), nitrous oxide (N2O), ozone and fluorinated gases including CFCs, HFCs, PFCs, SF6 and NF3.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.topic: Climate Change and Global Environmental Issues
questions.chapter: 3.10.6 Climate Change and Global Environmental Issues
questions.question: Which of the following is a consequence of ozone depletion?

options.A: More UV-B radiation reaching Earth's surface

questions.explanation: Ozone depletion increases harmful UV-B reaching the surface.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.topic: Climate Change and Global Environmental Issues
questions.chapter: 3.10.6 Climate Change and Global Environmental Issues
questions.question: Which of the following is a consequence of ocean acidification?

options.A: Lower pH and reduced carbonate availability

questions.explanation: Ocean acidification leads to lower pH and reduced carbonate availability, making shell and skeleton formation harder for corals and some shell-forming organisms.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.topic: Climate Change and Global Environmental Issues
questions.chapter: 3.10.6 Climate Change and Global Environmental Issues
questions.question: Which of the following is a consequence of desertification?

options.A: Loss of land productivity and ecological function

questions.explanation: Desertification leads to loss of land productivity and ecological function.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.topic: Climate Change and Global Environmental Issues
questions.chapter: 3.10.6 Climate Change and Global Environmental Issues
questions.question: Which of the following is a key driver of global warming?
questions.explanation: Global warming is driven by the enhanced greenhouse effect, which causes an increase in global mean surface temperature.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.topic: Climate Change and Global Environmental Issues
questions.chapter: 3.10.6 Climate Change and Global Environmental Issues
questions.question: Which of the following is a key driver of ozone depletion?
questions.explanation: Ozone depletion is driven by ozone-depleting substances releasing halogens, which leads to more UV-B reaching Earth's surface.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.topic: Climate Change and Global Environmental Issues
questions.chapter: 3.10.6 Climate Change and Global Environmental Issues
questions.question: Which of the following is a key driver of acid rain?

options.A: SO2 and NOx transformed into acids

questions.explanation: Acid rain is driven by SO2 and NOx transformed into acids, leading to acidification and material damage.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following correctly matches an instrument with its adoption year?
questions.explanation: UNEP was established in 1972; IPCC in 1988; UNFCCC was adopted in 1992 (in force 1994).

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following correctly matches an instrument with its core focus?

options.A: Ramsar Convention—wetlands conservation and wise use
options.B: CITES—international trade in listed wildlife species

questions.explanation: Ramsar focuses on wetlands; CITES on international trade in listed wildlife species; Montreal Protocol on ozone-depleting substances.

questions.subject: Environmental Geography and Ecology
questions.question: Which of the following correctly matches an instrument with its core focus?

options.C: CBD—biodiversity conservation, sustainable use and benefit-sharing
